opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different lenses I use, and none of them is fully satisfying on its own.

The first, and probably the one I lean on most, is looking at the length of tasks AI systems can complete autonomously. There's been work measuring the time horizon of software and research-adjacent tasks that models can do with, say, 50% reliability, meaning how long those tasks take a skilled human. That horizon has been doubling roughly every several months, maybe faster recently. If you extrapolate that trend, you can ask: when do we get to systems that can reliably do tasks that take a human engineer weeks or months? That's roughly the regime where you could plausibly hand off large chunks of AI R&D. Naive extrapolation gets you there in a handful of years, though there's a lot of uncertainty about whether the trend holds, and about how well these benchmark tasks transfer to messy real-world research.

The second lens is more qualitative: talking to people at AI companies and seeing how much they actually use these systems in their own work. Are researchers delegating real engineering tasks? Are they getting a meaningful speedup, or does the AI mostly help with boilerplate? My sense is that the speedup on coding-heavy work is real but still modest overall. A lot of what bottlenecks research is research taste: deciding which experiments to run, interpreting results, noticing when something is subtly broken. Models are weaker there than at raw implementation.

That gets at a subtlety I care about. "Automating AI R&D" isn't one threshold. There's a big difference between a system that can replace a junior research engineer and one that can replace your best research scientists. You could fully automate the engineering side and still be bottlenecked on compute for experiments and on top-level judgment. So I try to break it down: what fraction of the work could be automated, and how much does that actually accelerate overall progress, given that compute stays fixed in the short run?

The third thing I watch is benchmark trends on harder agentic and research-style evaluations, things like reproducing ML papers or doing open-ended engineering in realistic codebases. I hold those somewhat loosely because benchmarks saturate and get gamed, but the direction is informative.

Putting it together, my rough view is that there's a substantial chance, maybe something like a quarter to a third, that we get systems capable of fully automating AI research engineering within the next few years, with a longer tail beyond that. I want to stress the uncertainty. These trends could slow, especially if progress has been propped up by things like scaling reinforcement learning on easily verifiable tasks that don't generalize to the fuzzier parts of research. But I don't think you can confidently rule out short timelines, and from a safety perspective that's the key point. If there's a meaningful chance we're only a few years from AIs doing most of the work of building better AIs, we should be preparing for that now.

r001.rationale: The response extrapolates recent task-horizon growth, but does not propose estimating capabilities four years ahead from gains over the preceding four years.

r002.rationale: It mentions a horizon doubling every several months and extrapolating to tasks lasting weeks or months in a handful of years; it does not give the eight- or sixteen-hour task estimate or the slightly-under-two-year timeframe.

r003.rationale: The response says week- or month-long tasks could allow handing off large chunks of AI R&D, but does not clearly connect weeklong-task capability to being close to automating a research engineer’s job with additional practical work.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it, the thing I actually care about is: when do we get AI systems that can basically do the job of an AI researcher at a frontier lab, end to end? Not just write some code when you hand them a well-specified task, but notice what the interesting problem is, run experiments for weeks, interpret the results, change course when things don't work. That's the milestone that matters, because once you have that, you can run a huge number of copies and progress potentially gets a lot faster.

So then the question is, how do I use what I'm seeing to estimate the distance to that? And I'd say there are a few things I lean on.

The first is the horizon-length picture, which METR has been tracking. The basic idea is: take tasks that a human expert would take some amount of time to do, and ask how long a task can the AI reliably complete. A few years ago that was tasks that would take a person a couple of minutes. Then it was tens of minutes, then hours. And the striking thing is that it has been roughly doubling on some fairly consistent timescale, something like every six or seven months, and more recently it's looked a bit faster than that. If you just naively extrapolate, you get to AI handling tasks that take humans weeks or months within a handful of years. And "a month-long task" is pretty close to "a research project."

Now, I want to be careful here, because I think the naive extrapolation can mislead you in both directions. On the one hand, the benchmarks are cleaner than real work. The tasks have clear success criteria, they're in a fixed environment, there's no messy context you have to go gather from colleagues. Real research is a lot more open-ended, and my sense is that current models still fall over in ways that are kind of embarrassing when you put them in that setting. They get stuck, they don't notice they're stuck, they confidently do the wrong thing. So the measured horizon probably overstates what they can do in practice.

On the other hand, the trend doesn't have to continue at the same rate. It could slow down because we run out of easy wins, or because the kind of thing that's needed for long-horizon agency is just qualitatively different from what we've been scaling. But it could also speed up, because as the models get more useful for AI research itself, you start getting a feedback loop. And I think we're already seeing early versions of that. People at the labs are using these systems a lot for writing code and running experiments, and I think they're getting a meaningful speedup, even if it's not yet the dramatic thing.

The second thing I look at is just, qualitatively, what are the failures? When I look at what the best models get wrong now, is it the kind of thing where it's obvious how you'd fix it with more scale and more RL on agentic tasks? Or is it the kind of thing where I think, "Huh, I don't know how you'd get there from here"? And honestly, over the last couple of years, most of the failures have shifted from the second category into the first. Things like "it can't stay coherent over a long task" used to seem fundamental, and now it looks more like a thing that's steadily improving with training.

The third thing is the inputs. Compute is still going up fast, and the labs have figured out that you can get a lot of mileage out of reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, which is exactly the sort of thing that coding and a lot of ML research is. So I expect continued strong progress on precisely the capabilities that matter for automating AI R&D, maybe more so than on, say, being a good novelist.

So if you put all that together, where do I land? My median for "AI can fully automate the job of an AI researcher" is something like a few years out, maybe four-ish, with pretty wide error bars. I'd put a meaningful probability, maybe twenty-five percent or so, on it happening within two to three years, and I think it's also very plausible it takes a decade or more because the long-horizon, messy-context stuff turns out to be harder than the trend suggests.

And I'd stress that I'm not that confident. The main thing I'd say is that the evidence has been consistently pointing in the direction of "sooner than people thought a few years ago," and I update somewhat on that, but I try not to be the person who just draws a straight line on a log plot and declares victory.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is to look at the actual tasks involved in AI research and ask how close models are to doing those, rather than treating progress on any one benchmark as a direct measure of how much time we have left.

There’s a lot of coding involved, so improvements in coding are pretty relevant. But there’s a big gap between writing a function when someone tells you exactly what it should do and carrying out a research project. You need to decide what experiment to run, understand whether the result is meaningful, debug things when they go wrong, and choose what to try next. Models can be useful at individual steps without being able to reliably manage that whole process.

So I’d put particular weight on whether they can complete longer, less well-specified tasks with less human intervention. Can you give a model a research objective and have it make progress over the course of a day? When it gets stuck, does it recover, or does a human need to supply the key insight?

And I’d distinguish fully automating research from substantially accelerating it. You could get a meaningful speedup while humans are still setting the direction and handling some bottlenecks. That speedup could then help produce better AI systems, which makes extrapolating the recent rate of progress tricky. Progress in capabilities is evidence that we’re getting closer, but translating it into a date depends a lot on which remaining difficulties turn out to be bottlenecks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using task performance to assess progress, but does not propose extrapolating the preceding four years of capability gains to estimate capabilities four years ahead.

r002.rationale: It asks whether a model can make progress on a research objective over a day, but gives no doubling-time extrapolation or estimate for eight- or sixteen-hour tasks in under two years.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention weeklong tasks or say that completing them could bring AI close to automating a research engineer’s job.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how well current systems can do the actual tasks involved in AI research, and how quickly that’s improving. Coding ability is a pretty important input, because a lot of AI research consists of implementing experiments, debugging them, and interpreting the results. So recent progress on coding should update us toward automation being closer.

But there’s a substantial gap between being able to solve a well-specified programming problem and being able to autonomously carry out a research project. You need to choose useful experiments, notice when something has gone wrong, and make progress over a long sequence of actions without someone continually steering you. A system can be very impressive on short tasks and still fail badly at that.

I’d therefore put a lot of weight on experiments where you give systems realistic research tasks and see how much human assistance they need. Can they reproduce a result? Can they improve an existing training setup? Can they come up with an idea, test it, and correctly decide whether it worked?

And we don’t necessarily need to automate all of that before things start moving substantially faster. If AI systems automate a large fraction of the implementation work, researchers can run more experiments. Then the question is how much the remaining bottlenecks matter. So I’d distinguish full automation from substantial acceleration, and I’d expect us to see the latter first.
